summary: Defines Applicability Statement 2 (AS2), a way to exchange structured business data securely over HTTP, using MIME for packaging. The data may be XML, EDI, or other formats. It parallels the SMTP-based approach in RFC 3335 but sends data directly between peers over HTTP.

eli5.summary: Two companies want to mail each other secure order forms. This memo explains how to put the forms in a sealed envelope and deliver it straight over the web, so each side knows it arrived safely.

subtitle: Sending signed, encrypted business documents straight over HTTP and getting a signed receipt back.

tldr.problem: Trading partners that exchange EDI or XML business documents want them to travel securely over HTTP, with proof of who sent them and proof that they arrived intact, rather than over the SMTP route in RFC 3335.
tldr.mechanism: AS2 packages the document as MIME inside an HTTP POST, optionally signed and encrypted with S/MIME. The receiver answers with a Message Disposition Notification (MDN), signed if requested, that carries a hash of what it received.
tldr.outcome: The sender who keeps its records and checks the signed receipt has strong evidence of delivery, which the RFC calls non-repudiation of receipt. Every security feature is optional per trading relationship.

facts.label: Security combinations
facts.value: 12 possible; only the last gives the full loop

today: RFC 4130 is a Proposed Standard from July 2005. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: What AS2 Is
sections.content:
RFC 4130 is an applicability statement: it does not invent new protocols but says how existing ones fit together. It describes how to exchange structured business data securely over HTTP instead of SMTP. The data may be XML, EDI in ANSI X12 or UN/EDIFACT format, or any other format describable in MIME. The SMTP version is "AS1" in RFC 3335, which is why this one is informally called AS2.

It builds on RFC 2616 (HTTP), RFC 1767 (EDI content types), RFC 3023 (XML types), RFC 1847 (signed and encrypted MIME), RFC 3462 (multipart/report), RFC 3798 (MDNs) and S/MIME 3.1 (RFC 3851 and RFC 3852). The authors say they are trying to re-invent as little as possible. The goal is interoperability between business-to-business user agents.
sections.eli5: This memo does not invent a new language. It says how to combine several existing ones so two companies can swap secret papers over the web.

sections.title: The Secure Transmission Loop
sections.content:
The full security story is a loop. The sender signs and encrypts the document with S/MIME and asks for a signed receipt. The sender keeps a record of the message, its Message-ID and its digest, called the MIC (message integrity check). The receiver decrypts, checks the signature, and returns a signed receipt that contains the hash of what it got.

When the sender verifies that signed receipt and sees the MIC match its own record, a "legal event" called non-repudiation of receipt (NRR) occurs. The RFC calls NRR an outcome of holding the right evidence, not a technical message.

Users can choose how much of this to use. Encrypted or not, signed or not, with no receipt, an unsigned receipt or a signed receipt gives twelve combinations. Only the last one, encrypted and signed data with a signed receipt, gives the whole suite of features. For signatures, SHA-1 is RECOMMENDED for outgoing messages and both MD5 and SHA-1 should be supported for incoming ones.
sections.eli5: You lock and sign a box, send it, and keep a note of what you put in. The other side sends back a signed card that describes the box. If the card matches your note, you can prove it arrived.

sections.title: Message Structure and AS2 Headers
sections.content:
An AS2 message is MIME inside an HTTP message, plus a few AS2 headers. The nesting depends on the choices: plain content, multipart/signed with an application/pkcs7-signature part, application/pkcs7-mime for encryption, or both together. Implementations MUST support, among others, multipart/signed, multipart/report, message/disposition-notification, the PKCS7 types, and the EDI-X12, EDIFACT, edi-consent and XML application types.

The sender uses an HTTP POST. HTTP can carry binary data, so MIME content transfer encodings are not needed. The receiver must not fail just because that header is missing.

AS2 adds three headers. AS2-Version is 1.0 for this specification, and 1.1 marks support for compression as defined by RFC 3274. AS2-From and AS2-To identify the partners with names of 1 to 128 printable ASCII characters. These are case-sensitive and must not be folded. A reply swaps them, so the response's To matches the request's From. The Message-Id has a maximum length of 998 characters, and SHOULD be 255 or fewer.
sections.eli5: The envelope has labels saying who it is from and who it is for. Inside, it is sealed and signed in whatever way the two companies agreed.

sections.title: Receipts: Synchronous and Asynchronous MDNs
sections.content:
A receipt is a Message Disposition Notification (MDN). To request one the sender includes Disposition-notification-to, whose address is required but ignored by the receiver. To request a signed one it adds Disposition-notification-options with signed-receipt-protocol and signed-receipt-micalg, both REQUIRED for a signed receipt. The only protocol value is pkcs7-signature, and the algorithms are sha1 and md5.

A synchronous MDN comes back in the HTTP response on the same connection. For an asynchronous MDN the sender adds Receipt-Delivery-Option with a URL. The receiver first sends a plain HTTP response saying whether the transfer worked, and later POSTs the MDN to that URL, which may be on a different host.

Synchronous gives immediate confirmation but a large message may take longer to process than the connection is allowed to stay open. Asynchronous returns quickly, but the MDN must carry enough to identify the original message.

A signed MDN is multipart/signed: the first part is a multipart/report and the second is the signature. It includes Original-Message-ID and Received-content-MIC, the base64 digest followed by the algorithm. When a signed receipt is requested, the receiver MUST return one, and the user must not be allowed to configure the agent to refuse.
sections.eli5: The reply card either comes back while you wait at the door, or the other company mails it to you later at an address you gave. Either way it says what it got.

sections.title: Disposition Values and Retries
sections.content:
The MDN's Disposition field reports what happened. Normal success is automatic-action/MDN-sent-automatically; processed. Problems that are not about the content use processed plus a modifier. The defined errors are decryption-failed, authentication-failed, integrity-check-failed and unexpected-processing-error. A warning is allowed when processing continued anyway. The failed type is used when an MDN cannot properly be produced, such as when the requested MIC algorithm is unsupported.

Even when the data was rejected for a security reason, the HTTP status SHOULD still indicate success at the HTTP level, because the outcome is in the MDN. A signed receipt request is honored even if the content has an error.

If a client cannot read the server's response and the cause is transient, it SHOULD repeat the POST with identical content, including the same Message-ID. Servers SHOULD expect repeats and resend the earlier reply. Retry intervals and counts are left to the trading partner agreement.
sections.eli5: The reply card has a status line like 'all fine', 'could not unlock it' or 'could not tell who sent it'. If your delivery vanishes, you send the same one again.

sections.title: Certificates and Trust
sections.content:
AS2 does not define how partners find each other's keys. In the near term, exchanging and certifying public keys MUST be handled as part of setting up the trading partnership, and the software keeps a database of those keys. X.509 certificates are REQUIRED, but a certification authority is not. Partners may self-certify, and certificates may be self-signed.

The RFC adds that, in the long term, further standards may simplify setting up a partnership, including third-party authentication of partners.
sections.eli5: The two companies swap their lock keys in person or by agreement ahead of time, not through some central key office.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Most of the document is itself about security, and the section quotes the S/MIME specifications. It repeats that 40-bit encryption is considered weak and offers little real security over plaintext, and that failures in certificate checking, such as an expired or revoked certificate or an untrusted chain, must be noticed and reported to the user.

On non-repudiation it cautions that this specification does not itself define NRR, since that is a business or legal matter. For strict NRR, digital signatures on both the original message and the receipt are the RECOMMENDED mechanism. If the original message is unsigned, some other authentication must accompany the request, such as client-side SSL, IPsec, or HTTP authentication over SSL. Records of content, security basis and digest must be kept.

For HTTPS, server certificates with or without the URL in the Common Name, self-signed and CA-certified, MUST be supported. Replays are expected to be dropped by normal duplicate detection using Message-Id or business transaction identifiers.
sections.eli5: Weak locks are almost as bad as no lock. To prove a delivery later, both sides must sign things and keep their notes safe.

items.label: decryption-failed
items.desc: The receiver could not decrypt the message contents.

items.label: authentication-failed
items.desc: The receiver could not authenticate the sender.

items.label: integrity-check-failed
items.desc: The receiver could not verify content integrity.

items.label: unexpected-processing-error
items.desc: Catch-all for any other processing errors.
